_comment: QuantPrep study notes — seed content for the Math Academy-style learning layer. One entry per topic id. `body` is markdown. `prereqs` lists prerequisite topic ids (edit to match your approved knowledge graph). `source` marks these as human-authored so the app won't overwrite them with AI drafts without confirmation.

notes.title: Basic Probability & Expected Value
notes.body:
## Core idea
Probability measures how likely an event is (0 to 1). Expected value is the long-run average of a random quantity — a weighted average of outcomes by their probabilities.

## When to use (trigger)
Any time you're asked "what's the chance of..." or "on average, how many/how much...". This is the foundation every other probability topic builds on.

## Key formulas
- $P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}$ (equally likely case)
- $E[X] = \sum_i x_i \, P(x_i)$ — sum each outcome times its probability
- Independent events: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$
- Mutually exclusive: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$

## Worked example
Fair coin: win £2 on heads, lose £1 on tails. Expected profit per flip:
$$E = \tfrac{1}{2}(2) + \tfrac{1}{2}(-1) = 1 - 0.5 = £0.50$$

## Common mistakes
- **Adding when you should multiply**: "A and B both happen" multiplies; "A or B happens" (exclusive) adds.
- **Confusing a count with a probability**: the number of arrangements (e.g. 3) is not the probability (e.g. 3/8).
- Forgetting outcomes aren't always equally likely.

notes.title: Geometric Distribution
notes.body:
## Core idea
Models how many independent trials you need until the **first success**, where every trial has the same success probability $p$.

## When to use (trigger)
"Repeat independent trials until the first success." Coin until heads, die until a six, free throws until a basket.

## Key formula
$$E = \frac{1}{p}$$

## Key properties
- **Memoryless**: past failures don't change the expected wait. Flipped 10 tails? Still expect 2 more flips to get heads.
- Only valid when $p$ is **constant** across trials.

## Worked example
Roll a die until you get a 1 or 2. Success prob $p = 2/6 = 1/3$, so $E = 1/p = 3$ rolls.

## Common mistakes
- **Drawing without replacement is NOT geometric** — $p$ changes each draw. Use the without-replacement shortcut or enumeration instead.
- **"Any match" problems**: for two dice showing the same number, $p = 1/6$ (condition on the first die), not $1/36$.
- Confusing $E = 1/p$ (a count of trials) with $p$ itself.

notes.title: Enumerate Scenarios
notes.body:
## Core idea
When probabilities change each step (dependent trials) and there are only a few possible outcomes, list every scenario, find each one's probability, and combine.

## When to use (trigger)
Drawing without replacement, dependent events, small number of ways the process can end.

## Key formula
$$E = \sum_n n \cdot P(\text{ends on trial } n)$$

## Steps
1. List every scenario (ends on trial 1, 2, 3, ...).
2. Multiply the conditional probabilities **along each path**.
3. Sanity check: the scenario probabilities must sum to 1.
4. Compute the weighted sum.

## Worked example
3 red, 2 blue balls, draw without replacement until first blue:
- P(blue draw 1) = 2/5
- P(blue draw 2) = (3/5)(2/4) = 3/10
- P(blue draw 3) = (3/5)(2/4)(2/3) = 1/5
- P(blue draw 4) = (3/5)(2/4)(1/3)(2/2) = 1/10
- Sum = 1 ✓, and $E = 1(2/5)+2(3/10)+3(1/5)+4(1/10) = 2$

## Common mistakes
- **Multiply along a path, don't add.**
- On the final draw the target is often guaranteed (probability 1) — e.g. 2/2, not 1/2.
- Too many scenarios? Look for the shortcut instead.

notes.title: First Success Without Replacement (Shortcut)
notes.body:
## Core idea
A symmetry shortcut for the expected position of the first "success" when drawing without replacement — no enumeration needed.

## When to use (trigger)
$N$ total items, $k$ of them are "successes", drawing without replacement, want the expected draw of the **first** success.

## Key formula
$$E[\text{first}] = \frac{N+1}{k+1}$$

For the **last** success, flip it: use the count of the *other* type and measure from the far end.

## Intuition
$k$ successes split the $N$ items into $k+1$ equal gaps by symmetry. The first success sits just past the first gap.

## Worked examples
- 3 red, 2 blue, first blue: $E = (5+1)/(2+1) = 2$ ✓ (matches enumeration)
- 4 red, 2 blue, first blue: $E = 7/3 \approx 2.33$
- 1 blue among 5: $E = 6/2 = 3$ (middle, by symmetry)

## Common mistakes
- Using this **with replacement** — then it's geometric ($1/p$) instead.
- Plugging in the wrong $k$ (it's the count of the type you're waiting for).
- Forgetting the $+1$s.

notes.title: Complementary Counting
notes.body:
## Core idea
"At least one" is hard to count directly (too many cases). Compute the probability of the **opposite** event and subtract from 1.

## When to use (trigger)
"At least one / at least two" where a direct count would mean summing many cases.

## Key formula
$$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})$$

## Steps
1. Compute $P(\text{opposite})$ — usually one clean chain of fractions.
2. **Multiply** the chain (you need every step to hold), don't add.
3. Subtract from 1.

## Worked example
Birthday problem, 30 people, P(at least two share):
$$1 - \frac{365}{365}\cdot\frac{364}{365}\cdots\frac{336}{365} \approx 70\%$$
The surprising 70% is the "birthday paradox".

## Common mistakes
- **Adding the chain instead of multiplying.**
- Stopping the chain too early (it runs over all the people/items).
- Forgetting the first term is 365/365 = 1 (the first person is unconstrained).

notes.title: Symmetry / Condition on First Step
notes.body:
## Core idea
When you don't care *which* specific outcome, fix the first item as a free reference point and ask what the rest must do to match it. Symmetry often gives the answer with no calculation.

## When to use (trigger)
"Any match / any double / any pair", or setups where interchangeable parts make outcomes equally likely.

## Key idea
First item lands anywhere (probability 1). Then compute the probability the others match/relate to it.

## Worked example
Two dice, probability of any double: first die lands anywhere, second must match → $1/6$. (Equivalently, 6 doubles out of 36 outcomes.)

## Classic trap
- $1/36$ = probability of a **specific** double (both 3s).
- $1/6$ = probability of **any** double.

## Common mistakes
- Multiplying $1/6 \times 1/6$ when you only need a match, not a specific value.
- Missing an available symmetry and grinding a long calculation instead.

notes.title: Gambler's Ruin
notes.body:
## Core idea
A random walk moving ±1 each step. What's the probability of hitting an upper target before a lower one (ruin)?

## When to use (trigger)
"Reach +N before going broke at −N", random up/down moves.

## Key formulas
Boundary conditions (always start here): $p(-N)=0$ (broke), $p(+N)=1$ (won).

Fair coin, start at $k$, boundaries $\pm N$:
$$p(k) = \frac{k+N}{2N}$$

Unfair coin ($q=1-p$):
$$p(k) = \frac{1-(q/p)^{k+N}}{1-(q/p)^{2N}}$$

## Worked example
Start £0, win at +£3, lose at −£3, fair coin. You start exactly halfway, coin is fair → by symmetry $p(0) = 1/2$.

## Common mistakes
- Trying to calculate the boundaries instead of reading them off (0 and 1).
- Forgetting this asks for a **probability of ruin**, not an expected value.
- Overcomplicating the fair symmetric case, which is just 1/2.

notes.title: Staged Geometric (Coupon Collector)
notes.body:
## Core idea
Collecting all $n$ distinct types. Break the wait into stages; each stage is its own geometric distribution; add up the expected waits.

## When to use (trigger)
"See every outcome at least once" / "collect all n types".

## Key formula
$$E = \frac{n}{n} + \frac{n}{n-1} + \dots + \frac{n}{1} = n\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{k}$$

## Steps
1. Stage 1: any new type, $p_1 = n/n = 1$, expected = 1.
2. Stage 2: need a new one, $p_2 = (n-1)/n$, expected = $n/(n-1)$.
3. ... continue to stage $n$ where only 1 type is left, $p_n = 1/n$, expected = $n$.
4. Sum all stages (uses linearity of expectation).

## Worked example
Roll a die until all six faces seen: $E = 6(1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/6) \approx 14.7$ rolls.

## Common mistakes
- Trying $(1/n)^n$ or a single geometric — it's a **sum of stages**.
- Forgetting each stage flips $p$ into $1/p$ for its expected wait.

notes.title: Bayes' Theorem
notes.body:
## Core idea
Update a belief after observing evidence. Combines a base rate (prior) with how likely the evidence is under each hypothesis.

## When to use (trigger)
"You observed X — what's the probability of underlying cause Y?", test-accuracy + rare-condition problems, "given X happened, P(Y)?".

## Best interview method: population table
1. Pick a round number of trials (100, 300, 1000).
2. Split into groups by the prior.
3. Apply the likelihoods to get counts.
4. Answer = (count you want) / (total count matching the observation).

## Formal formula
$$P(A|B) = \frac{P(B|A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$$

## Worked example
Disease affects 1%, test 90% accurate, you test positive. Out of 1000: 10 sick → 9 test positive; 990 healthy → 99 false positives. $P(\text{sick}\,|\,+) = 9/108 \approx 8.3\%$. Base rate dominates.

## Classic traps
- "At least one child is a boy, P(both boys)?" = 1/3 (three cases: BB, BG, GB).
- "The **older** child is a boy, P(both boys)?" = 1/2 (pins down a specific child — more information).

## Common mistakes
- Answering with the test accuracy (90%) instead of the posterior (8.3%).
- Counting all sick people rather than only those matching the observation (9, not 10).

notes.title: Conditional Probability
notes.body:
## Core idea
The probability of A **given** that B has happened. Conditioning restricts the sample space to the outcomes where B holds.

## When to use (trigger)
"Given that...", "if we know...", any time information updates the odds. Prerequisite for Bayes and recursive states.

## Key formula
$$P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}$$

## Worked example
Two children, at least one is a boy. Sample space {BB, BG, GB, GG}; condition on "at least one boy" removes GG, leaving 3 equally likely cases; P(both boys) = 1/3.

## Common mistakes
- Treating "at least one is a boy" the same as "the older is a boy" (1/3 vs 1/2) — what the condition pins down matters.
- Forgetting to shrink the denominator to only the conditioned outcomes.

notes.title: Combinatorics (Permutations & Combinations)
notes.body:
## Core idea
Counting arrangements and selections. The one decision that matters: **does order matter?**

## When to use (trigger)
"How many ways", "how many arrangements", "how many hands".

## Key formulas
- Permutations (order matters): $P(n,k) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-k)!}$
- Combinations (order doesn't): $\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$
- Binomial probability (exactly $k$ successes in $n$ trials): $\binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$

## Decision rule
- "Arrange / line up / rank" → permutation.
- "Choose / select / committee" → combination.

## "Exactly k of a special type" pattern
$$\binom{\text{special}}{k} \times \binom{\text{remaining}}{\text{rest}}$$

## Worked examples
- Arrange 4 letters: $4! = 24$.
- Choose 2 from 5: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$.
- Exactly 2 aces in a 5-card hand: $\binom{4}{2}\binom{48}{3} = 103{,}776$.

## Common mistakes
- Grabbing numbers from a previous problem — restate first.
- Computing a probability when asked for a count (or vice versa).
- Using combinations when order actually matters.

notes.title: Pigeonhole Principle
notes.body:
## Core idea
If $n+1$ items go into $n$ boxes, at least one box holds 2 or more. Simple to state; the skill is spotting the boxes.

## When to use (trigger)
"Prove that at least two must share / match / collide."

## Steps
1. Define the boxes (categories).
2. Count boxes ($n$) and items ($n+1$ or more).
3. Conclude.

## Worked examples
- 13 people → two share a birth month (12 months = boxes).
- Pick 6 numbers from 1–10 → two sum to 11. Boxes are the pairs {1,10},{2,9},{3,8},{4,7},{5,6} = 5 boxes; 6 picks force a collision.

## Common mistakes
- Not realising you sometimes have to **construct** the boxes (e.g. pairs summing to 11), they're not always obvious.
- Miscounting boxes vs items.

notes.title: Linearity of Expectation
notes.body:
## Core idea
The expected value of a sum equals the sum of expected values — **even when the pieces are dependent**. This is what makes it so powerful.

## When to use (trigger)
A complex expected-value problem that looks impossible to compute directly. Break the whole into small pieces.

## Key formula
$$E[X_1 + \dots + X_n] = E[X_1] + \dots + E[X_n]$$

## Three steps
1. Define individual pieces (indicators): each person, pair, roll, adjacent slot.
2. Find $P$ for one piece (usually easy).
3. Multiply by the number of pieces.

## Worked examples
- 10 people, random hats: $E = 10 \times \tfrac{1}{10} = 1$.
- 30 people, expected shared-birthday pairs: $\binom{30}{2}\times \tfrac{1}{365} \approx 1.19$.
- Deck of 52, expected Aces immediately before a King: $51 \times \tfrac{4}{52}\times \tfrac{4}{51} = \tfrac{4}{13}$.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking you need independence — you don't.
- Not spotting the right "piece" to sum over (adjacent pairs, individual people, etc.).

notes.title: Recursive States / Conditioning
notes.body:
## Core idea
Set up equations for the expected value from each "state" (how much progress you've made), based on what happens after one step. Solve simultaneously.

## When to use (trigger)
Sequential process where a setback can send you backward (waiting for a pattern like HH, random walks).

## Key structure
$$E_{\text{state}} = 1 + \sum_{\text{outcomes}} P(\text{outcome}) \times E_{\text{new state}}$$
The "1" is the step you just took; game-over states contribute 0.

## Worked example
Expected flips to get HH. States: 0 (no progress), 1 (one H). $E_1 = 1 + \tfrac12(0) + \tfrac12 E_0$; $E_0 = 1 + \tfrac12 E_1 + \tfrac12 E_0$. Solving gives $E_0 = 6$. (For HT, $E_0 = 4$ — a near miss doesn't reset you.)

## Common mistakes
- **Sign errors** when solving: collect all $E$ terms on one side *before* dividing.
- Choosing states by the full history instead of by progress toward the goal.
- Forgetting the "+1" for the current step.

notes.title: Continuous Distributions
notes.body:
## Core idea
The continuous analogues of discrete probability. Sums become integrals; probabilities become areas under a curve. Know three distributions and order statistics.

## When to use (trigger)
Uniform/normal/Poisson setups, "expected max/min", anything measured on a continuum.

## The three distributions
- **Uniform** $U(a,b)$: $E[X] = \tfrac{a+b}{2}$, $P(X<x) = \tfrac{x-a}{b-a}$.
- **Normal** $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$: 68% within $1\sigma$, 95% within $2\sigma$, 99.7% within $3\sigma$. Sum of independent normals is normal. Foundation of parametric VaR.
- **Poisson** $\text{Pois}(\lambda)$: $E[X]=\text{Var}(X)=\lambda$; counts rare events per period (defaults/year, trades/sec).

## Order statistics (uniform on [0,1])
$$E[\min] = \frac{1}{n+1}, \qquad E[\max] = \frac{n}{n+1}$$
Symmetric around 0.5; as $n$ grows, min→0 and max→1.

## Deeper (revisit after calculus refresh)
$P(\max < x) = x^n$ (all $n$ below $x$), differentiate for the PDF, integrate for $E[\max]$. The $P(\max<x)=x^n$ step is the key move.

## Common mistakes
- Reaching for a formula without the gap/symmetry intuition.
- Mixing up which is min vs max in the $\tfrac{k}{n+1}$ form.

notes.title: Out of the Box / Lateral Thinking
notes.body:
## Core idea
No formula applies. Find a hidden constraint, an invariant, or reframe the problem entirely.

## When to use (trigger)
Physical puzzles, logic puzzles, "how do you measure/achieve X" with odd constraints.

## Go-to moves
- **Small cases first** (n = 1, 2, 3) — the pattern usually shows by n = 3.
- **Odd/even parity** — many problems flip state each step.
- **Find what's expensive and minimise it** (bridge crossing: the slow people should cross together).
- **Look for an invariant** — something conserved regardless of choices.

## Worked examples
- Burning ropes → light both ends (halves burn time regardless of unevenness) → measure 45 min with two ropes.
- Bridge crossing (1,2,5,10 min, one torch) → pair the two slow people, use a fast runner as ferry → 17 min.
- Tiger & sheep (100 tigers) → even count → sheep is safe (parity argument).
- Card game (red pairs to you, black to dealer) → red pairs always equal black pairs → guaranteed tie → pay £0.
- Screwy pirates → work backward from 1 pirate, buy the cheapest votes → {98,1,0,1,0}.

## Common mistakes
- Reaching for expected-value machinery when the answer is a structural invariant.
- Getting the right answer with shaky reasoning (check parity/small cases explicitly).

notes.title: Derivatives & Greeks Intuition
notes.body:
## Core idea
Options interview questions lean far more on **intuition** — how a hedged book behaves, how a Greek moves, what a hedge forces you to trade — than on grinding through Black–Scholes. Almost every question in this topic is really asking: *do you know what the model is doing, and where it stops being true?*

## When to use (trigger)
"Which has higher gamma...", "you're delta-hedged and the stock gaps, what do you do", "how does a digital's price vary with vol", "reconcile this with put-call parity", "value it in ten seconds", "why is theta negative but the expected return positive".

## Key facts to have cold
- **Put-call parity**: $C - P = S - K e^{-rT}$. It is an arbitrage identity, not an approximation — reach for it whenever calls and puts are compared.
- **Delta** $= N(d_1)$: ~0.5 ATM (slightly above when $r>0$, since spot-ATM is in-the-money on a *forward* basis), $\to 1$ deep ITM call, $\to 0$ deep OTM. The pre-expiry graph is a smooth S-curve; the step function is delta *at* expiry.
- **$N(d_2)$** is the risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM. **$N(d_1)$** is the delta — a probability under a *different* measure. Different numbers, different meanings.
- **Gamma**: highest ATM and short-dated; $\propto 1/(S\sigma\sqrt{T})$.
- **Vega**: highest ATM and **long**-dated; $\propto S\sqrt{T}$. Opposite maturity profile to gamma — trade short-dated for gamma, long-dated for vega.
- **Theta**: the rent you pay for gamma. Worst for ATM near expiry.
- **ATM approximation**: $C \approx 0.4\,S\sigma\sqrt{T}$. Memorise it; it is what "value this in ten seconds" is testing. Equivalently, an ATM option is worth ~40% of a one-standard-deviation move.
- **Vol scales with $\sqrt{T}$**, never linearly. The quantity the model actually cares about is $\sigma\sqrt{T}$.
- **Delta-hedged daily P&L** $\approx \tfrac12\Gamma S^2\left[(\Delta S/S)^2 - \sigma^2 dt\right]$ — long gamma is long realised vol, short implied vol.
- **The PDE ties the Greeks together**: $\Theta + rS\Delta + \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma = rV$. With $r=0$ this is exactly $\Theta = -\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$, which is *why* theta and gamma have opposite signs — and why the rule can break when $r \neq 0$.

## Early exercise
- American **call** on a non-dividend payer = European. Exercising throws away time value *and* pays $K$ early, losing the interest. Sell it instead.
- American **put** can be exercised early: you *receive* $K$ early and earn interest on it, which beats the small residual optionality once deep ITM.
- Dividends are the only thing that makes early **call** exercise rational, and only at the last instant before an ex-dividend date, roughly when $D > K(1 - e^{-r(T-t)})$.

## Worked example (reasoning style)
Delta-hedged long a call; the stock gaps down sharply. Long the call means **short** delta shares. Spot falls, so $N(d_1)$ falls, so the hedge should be short *fewer* shares — you **buy** stock back, funded by borrowing. That is long gamma in one sentence: the hedge mechanically makes you buy low and sell high, and theta is the bill for it. Interviewers want this qualitative chain, not a number.

## Where Black–Scholes breaks (worth naming unprompted)
- **The smile/skew.** Implied vol is not a forecast; it is the number that forces the wrong model to return the right price. A non-flat plot is the model failing in an informative way — fat tails, negative skew from the leverage effect and crash risk, plus persistent demand for downside protection.
- **Discrete rebalancing and gaps.** Delta hedging only replicates in the continuous limit. This is why stop-loss hedging fails: Brownian paths cross the strike infinitely often, and the crossing cost converges to the option premium rather than to zero.
- **Barriers.** Near a barrier, delta can exceed 1 or flip sign. Hedging a barrier book by the book can lose more than not hedging.
- **Mean reversion** makes terminal variance grow sub-linearly, so long-dated options are worth less than a constant-vol model says.

## Common mistakes
- Reciting formulas when they want the mechanism ("explain carefully" → talk through the *why*).
- Forgetting that parity links calls and puts — most "paradoxes" here dissolve with one line of parity.
- Confusing $N(d_1)$ with $N(d_2)$, or delta-at-expiry with delta-before-expiry.
- Scaling vol linearly with time.
- Using **real-world** probabilities in a binomial tree. Build $q$ from the martingale condition; the stated probabilities are almost always a trap.
- Treating theta as a comparison between two options rather than the decay of a fixed one.

## Note
Your vol-surface / smile-strangle work gives you real texture here — lean on it.

notes.title: VaR & Risk Theory
notes.body:
## Core idea
Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall quantify portfolio risk. Know the three VaR methods, their trade-offs, and how the models get validated.

## When to use (trigger)
Risk-role interviews: "walk me through VaR methods", "why ES over VaR", "how do you backtest a VaR model".

## The three VaR methods
- **Parametric (variance–covariance)**: assumes normal returns; fast but misses fat tails.
- **Historical simulation**: replays past returns; no distributional assumption but backward-looking.
- **Monte Carlo**: simulate paths from a model; flexible but compute-heavy and model-dependent.

## Expected Shortfall (ES)
Average loss **beyond** the VaR threshold. Coherent (subadditive), unlike VaR; replaced VaR under FRTB.

## Backtesting
- **Kupiec** test: are the number of exceptions consistent with the confidence level?
- **Christoffersen** test: are exceptions independent (not clustered)?

## Key intuition
Base rates and tails dominate. Parametric VaR underestimates tail risk when returns are fat-tailed; correlations tend to →1 in stress, killing diversification just when you need it.

## Common mistakes
- Describing VaR as the worst case — it's a **threshold**, ES describes the tail beyond it.
- Forgetting VaR isn't subadditive (can penalise diversification).

## Note
Your clearinghouse MC-VaR work is a strong, concrete talking point — have it ready.

notes.title: Statistics
notes.body:
## Core idea
The descriptive and inferential toolkit underneath risk modelling: distributions, moments, correlation, hypothesis testing, time-series basics.

## When to use (trigger)
"Estimate/ test / regress" questions, fat tails, volatility clustering, correlation behaviour.

## Key facts
- **Mean / variance / covariance**: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$; covariance drives portfolio risk.
- **Correlation** is covariance normalised to [−1, 1]; it breaks down (→1) in stress.
- **Fat tails / kurtosis**: real returns have more extreme moves than the normal predicts — why parametric VaR under-warns.
- **Volatility clustering** (GARCH): big moves follow big moves.
- **Hypothesis testing**: null vs alternative, p-values, type I/II errors.

## Worked intuition
Why does historical VaR understate risk in a calm-then-crisis regime? Because the sample is dominated by calm data — the estimator is only as fat-tailed as its window.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming normality where tails are fat.
- Treating correlation as stable across regimes.
- Confusing variance of a sum with sum of variances when assets are correlated (the covariance term matters).
